titleStmt.title: Investigating the Effects of Schedulability Conditions on the Power Efficiency of Task Scheduling in an Embedded System

analytic.title: Investigating the Effects of Schedulability Conditions on the Power Efficiency of Task Scheduling in an Embedded System

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Power consumption, performance and reliability are the most important parameters in modern safety-critical distributed real-time embedded systems. This paper evaluates and compares different schedulability conditions in faulttolerant Rate-Monotonic (RM) and Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) algorithms, with respect to their power efficiency. The primary-backup scheme is used to implement fault tolerance in the algorithms. To evaluate the algorithms, a software tool is developed that can simulate an embedded system consisting of n processors and m periodic tasks. The results show that depending on the different schedulability conditions, the EDF algorithm implemented with the Best-Fit policy is on average 9.6% more power efficient than other algorithms when n=1500 and m=1000. between the two selected schedulability conditions in the RM algorithm, the Utilization Oriented (UO) condition implemented with the Best-Fit policy is on average 5% more power efficient than the other schedulability condition.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Embedded systems constitute the main part of digital systems, and play an important role in the modern life [1]. Many kinds of embedded systems are working in a real-time manner [10], where the correctness of the results depends not only on the logical correctness of results, but also on the time at which the results become available.

Two important issues in real-time systems are: 1) the ways by which tasks are assigned to processor(s), and 2) the ways by which tasks are scheduled. The first issue is done by using partitioning schemes [4] [12] [14] [20] joint with the schedulability conditions [13] [14] [20] and the second issue is done by using scheduling algorithms [6] [16]. Scheduling algorithms are divided into two types: 1) the fixed priority scheduling algorithms such as Rate-Monotonic (RM) algorithm, and 2) the dynamic priority scheduling algorithms such as Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) algorithm [2].

Power consumption and reliability are two important concerns in many safety-critical real-time embedded systems such as vehicular and medical embedded systems [1] [5]. In such systems power consumption is seriously affected by the increasing clock frequency and the circuit density [9] [17].

Several techniques to reduce power consumption are introduced; examples are Dynamic Voltage Scaling (DVS) [22], Dynamic Power Management (DPM) [21] and adaptive body biasing [7]. These techniques aim to lengthen the battery life for mobile embedded processors and decrease the associated cooling cost for embedded systems [25]. However, in above power reduction techniques, there is a tradeoff between power and performance. This means that the reduction of power consumption may damage the system performance [7] [21]. In such work, Power-Delay-Product (PDP) is used to measure the efficiency of power reduction methods.
In addition, reduction of power consumption may also decrease the reliability. This is because that a low-power system is more error susceptible than a system with ordinary power consumption [22].

Almost, all work related to schedulability conditions and scheduling algorithms are concentrated on the performance evaluation [2] [6] [12] [13]. Only a few work have considered either reliability [3] or power consumption [9] [15] [17] in their investigation. No one of the above work has paid attention to reliability and power consumption, simultaneously.
Previous researches related to partitioning schemes are also concentrated on the performance evaluation [3]. Here, power consumption and power efficiency are not studied.

The contribution of this paper can be divided into three points; 1) fault tolerance is implemented into different schedulability conditions for RM and EDF algorithms by using the Primary-Backup scheme [11] [18], and power efficiency of each condition is measured in term of PDP, 2) power efficiency of task partitioning schemes using the binpacking algorithm [4] [12] [14] [20] in joint with each of schedulability conditions are investigated in term of PDP, 3) the power efficiency of combination of each schedulability conditions with each task partitioning scheme are calculated and compared. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first attempt to do these comparisons and evaluations.

To evaluate and compare these algorithms, a software tool is developed that can simulate an embedded system consisting of n processors and m primary periodic tasks; in this experiment, n=1500 and m=1000.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses the tasks distribution policies in multiprocessor systems, and the schedulability conditions for different implementations of RM and EDF algorithms. In Section 3, the problem of reliability and fault tolerance in real-time embedded system is discussed and the Primary-Backup scheme as an approach for implementing fault tolerant and increasing the reliability and is explained. Moreover, in Section 4 the other important concern in embedded systems, i.e., Power consumption is explained, and the problem of ever-increasing power consumption is briefly reviewed. The system models, power model and fault model are shown in Section 5. The simulation method and simulation results are presented in Section 6 and Section 7, respectively. Finally, the conclusions are presented in Section 8.

div.head: II. TASKS DISTRIBUTION POLICIES
div.p: On a multiprocessor system the tasks could be distributed among processors either by the partitioning technique or the global technique. In the partitioning technique, each instance of a particular task is executed on the same processor, while in the global technique; each instance of a real-time task may be executed on different processors. Due to the intractability of optimal solution to the problem of partitioning [8], several heuristic methods for partitioning of tasks have been proposed; these methods are mainly based on the well-known bin-packing algorithm [4] [12] [14] [20]. In these studies the problem of partitioning and distributing tasks among processors are solved by combining any of the bin-packing policies with any of the schedulability conditions for the RM and EDF algorithms. Therefore, distributing tasks among processors are done by the well-known bin-packing heuristic policies and the decision of whether a processor is full or not is determined by the schedulability condition.

For the RM algorithm this set of algorithms can be described as NF,FF,BF,… ×{RM_Conditions}, Where NF (Next-Fit), FF (First-Fit) and BF (Best-Fit) are the binpacking heuristic methods and Worst-Case (WC) [13], and Utilization-Oriented (UO) [20] are the schedulability conditions for the RM algorithm.
For the EDF algorithm this set of algorithms can be described as NF,FF,BF,… ×{EDF_Condition}, The NF, BF and FF method are implemented as follows.
a) With the Best-Fit method, the best processor from utilization point of view will be nominated for scheduling the task on it.
b) With the Next-Fit method, the next Processor will be nominated for scheduling the task on it.
c) With the First-Fit method the first available processor will be nominated for scheduling the task on it.
After nominating the processor for scheduling the new task on it, the schedulability condition will check whether the task is schedulable or not.

div.head: A. Schedulability conditions
div.p: Schedulability conditions in each scheduling algorithm show the ability of scheduling a new task on a processor, in such manner that: 1) the new task can be completed before its deadline and 2) another scheduled task(s) which were known as schedulable do not miss its/their deadline.

div.head: III. RELIABILITY IN REAL-TIME EMBEDDED SYSTEMS
div.p: There are two main approaches to tolerate faults in task level in a real-time system. One of these approaches is Primary-Backup scheme. This approach allows execution of multiple copies of a task on different processors to tolerate processor and task failures [11] [18]. In this approach, the main task is called primary and the copy is called backup task.

There are three ways to implement the Primary-Backup Scheme [19]: 1) Primary-Backup exclusive, where primary and backup tasks are mutually exclusive in processor and time. 2) Primary-Backup concurrent, where primary and backup run at same time on different processors. 3) Primary-Backup overlapping, where primary and backup run on different processors with overlap in their execution time. This way is combination of the first and second ways.
This paper employs the Primary-Backup concurrent way to implement fault tolerance. If the acceptance test detects the primary task failure, the system relies on the output of the backup task.

div.head: IV. POWER CONSUMPTION IN REAL-TIME EMBEDDED
SYSTEMS
div.p: Another important concern in modern embedded systems is the power consumption. The power consumption could be divided into two components, i.e., dynamic and static (leakage) components. The dynamic component is the dominant power component [9], and is determined by the supply voltage and clock frequency. Thus, in case of decreasing the clock frequency and supply voltage it can be possible to reduce the power consumption at the cost of performance of the processors. This means that there is a tradeoff between reducing the power consumption and processor performance. For considering this tradeoff, power delay product is a suitable metric.

Also, there is a tradeoff between fault tolerance and power consumption in an embedded system, whereas a fault-tolerant system consumes more power than that a system without considering fault tolerance (because of implementing redundancy in the system). Furthermore, a low-power system is more error susceptible than a system with ordinary power consumption [22].
In this paper, the static and dynamic power components for each processor are calculated. The processors with no assigned task are assumed off during the simulation.

div.head: A. Task model
div.p: A set of n tasks ∑ = {τ 1 ,τ 2 ,…,τ n } are given with 4-tuple τ i =(c i ,r i ,d i ,T i ) for i=1,2,….,n where c i is the required execution time of task τ i . r i ,d i and T i are the arrival time, deadline and period of task τ i , respectively.
The following assumptions are used in the task model: i. Each task has a primary and a backup version for implementing fault tolerance requirement.
ii. Backup task must be scheduled on different processor than the primary task.

iii. The tasks are periodic and backup version will be created immediately upon tasks arrival. iv. For primary and backup versions of a task d i T i . v. The tasks are assumed to be independent from each other and they are preemptible.

vi. There are sufficient resources for both primary and backup versions of a task and there is no resource conflict between different versions of a task. vii. For each task the worst-case execution time takes into account.

div.head: B. Scheduler model
div.p: In a multiprocessor system, all the tasks arrive at a central controller and Then they will be distributed among the processors [16] [17]. This controller is called scheduler. The communication between the scheduler and the processors is through dispatch queues. Each processor has its own dispatch queue and the scheduling algorithms work on this queue. The duty of Scheduler is: to distribute tasks among processors according to the bin-packing heuristic method under RM or EDF schedulability conditions.
Admission control and the tasks assignment overheads will be ignored for the abovementioned algorithms. But the context switching overhead of scheduling algorithms is considered in this experiment.

div.head: C. Fault mode
div.p: The following assumptions are used in the fault model: i. In this paper, the system malfunctions are considered as processor failure or task failure. Thus, the causes of faults are not important.

ii. Faults are independent. iii. The scheduler is robustly designed. iv. Failure-detection mechanisms such as fail-signal and acceptance test are used to detect processors and tasks failures, respectively.
v. This paper assumes 100% failure detection coverage and zero failure detection Latency.

div.head: D. Power model
div.p: The following assumptions are used in the power model: i. The processors power consumption is divided into two components: 1) static power component and 2) dynamic power component.

ii. The dynamic power component is dominant in total power [23] [24]. Which is function of effective switching capacitance, supply voltage, and execution time of task τ i iii. The static power component is considered as the idle processor power consumption. Here it has been considered that an idle processor consumes 15% of the maximum possible power [9]. iv. Unused processors are off and consume power neither static nor dynamic.

div.head: VI. SIMULATION METHOD
div.p: This paper evaluates and compares fault-tolerant versions of two scheduling algorithms, i.e., EDF and RM algorithms with respect to the power efficiency of each algorithm.
For simulating the system, upon a task arrival, the primary and backup version of the task will be scheduled on different processors using one of the bin-packing partitioning policies (FF, BF or NF).

After assigning tasks to the processors, a procedure computes the dynamic and static power component for each processor plus the delay of each run and then the power delay product for each processor will be produced.

It is important to note that in periodic task scheduling, it has been proven that the release times of tasks do not affect the schedulability of the tasks [13]. Therefore, release time r i and deadline d i can be ignored in simulation and evaluation these algorithms.

div.head: VII. SIMULATION RESULTS
div.p: For simulating each implementation of algorithms, 1000 task were generated. On each task, T i is generated as a uniformly distributed variable with 10≤ T i 500 and c i is generated as a variable with exponential distribution in the range of 0<c i ≤αT i . α is defined as load factor, or the maximum allowable utilization of any task in the system.

Through applying the Primary-Backup scheme to the system, it was assumed that none of tasks (neither the primary version nor the backup version) will miss their deadline, and any tasks tolerate at least one failure.

Power Delay Product (PDP) is the metric to measure the power efficiency of the different implementations of the EDF and RM algorithms it is product of power consumption and the tasks completion delay. The power efficiency of the system is measured using four α values, i.e., α=0.25, α=0.5, α=0.75 and α~1.

The simulation results are shown in figure 1. Each part of this figure shows the simulation results for different faulttolerant implementations of abovementioned algorithms using the bin-packing policy distributing tasks into the multiprocessor system. The simulation results are shown for four different values of α. From each part of figure 1, it can be concluded that some algorithms yield best power efficiency only under certain α values. From the simulation results, it can be concluded that: a) Best-Fit bin-packing heuristic policy is the most power efficient approach for distribute tasks among processors.

b) Though the implementation of the Next-Fit binpacking heuristic policy is simpler than First-Fit and Best-Fit and has complexity of O(n), but this policy is the least power efficient policy among all mentioned bin-packing heuristic policies. This can be easily seen from the figure 1 that the results become worse with lower α values.
• For α =0.25, Next-Fit policy averagely has 44% power overhead than other partitioning policies.
• For α =0.5, Next-Fit policy averagely has 14% power overhead than other partitioning policies.
• For α =0.75, Next-Fit policy averagely has 8% power overhead than other partitioning policies.

• For α ~1, Next-Fit policy averagely has 7% power overhead than other partitioning policies. c) Although the implementation of EDF algorithm for scheduler is harder than the RM algorithm, it would be much better than the RM algorithm because the EDF algorithm have averagely 6% less PDP than the RM algorithm. • When α changes from 0.2 to 0.5, PDP increases by 23% • When α changes from 0.5 to 0.75, PDP increases by 6%
• When α changes from 0.75 to 0.99, PDP increases by 5% e) In term of power efficiency, the FF-EDF and BF-EDF are the best one.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, an evaluation of fault-tolerant versions of two well-known scheduling algorithms, i.e., The EDF, and RM algorithms, with respect to their power efficiency were presented.

To do this, a software tool was developed that can simulate an embedded system consisting of n processors and m primary tasks, and an embedded system consisting of 1500 processors and 1000 primary tasks was simulated by the tool. The implementation of mentioned algorithms on a multiprocessor system has been done by employing the binpacking algorithm for partitioning tasks on the processors. The fault-tolerant versions of these algorithms are based on using the primary-backup scheme within a multiprocessor embedded system. The dynamic and static components of power for the simulated multiprocessor system have been calculated by the tool.
The Results show that among the different implementations of the RM and EDF algorithms, the BF-EDF and FF-EDF have the best power efficiency.
